blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Large language model (LLM) agents are proposed for clinical prediction but are untested in pediatrics, where cohorts are small and outcomes are uncommon. Using records from 2,489 youth with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and 4,018 with type 1 diabetes (T1D), spanning structured data, note-derived social determinants and, in T1D, continuous glucose monitoring data, we predicted seven T2D outcomes, four also in T1D, at 24 months from 18 months of follow-up. CEDAR (Clinical Evidence-Driven Agent for Risk-prediction), an evidence-citing, self-auditing LLM pipeline, outperformed trained machine learning in both cohorts (pooled area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.815 versus 0.656 to 0.700 in T2D and 0.756 versus 0.603 to 0.631 in T1D), most on the sparsely screened outcomes. Only 4 of 70,246 values it cited did not match the chart. Reading only the evidence and reasoning cited by CEDAR, two pediatric endocrinologists reached the same prediction as CEDAR in about nine of ten cases, agreeing with each other on 90.5%.

blocks.en:
Diabetes is among the most common chronic diseases of childhood in the
United States. Type 1 diabetes (T1D) remains the predominant pediatric form
(prevalence ∼ \sim 215 per 100,000 under 20 years, incidence rising ∼ \sim 2%/year [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] ), while type 2 diabetes (T2D), once rare in youth, has
emerged as a parallel epidemic driven by childhood obesity (prevalence up
95% from 2001–2017, incidence ∼ \sim 18 per
100,000 [ 1 , 2 ] ). Youth of
Black, Hispanic, and American Indian descent bear a disproportionate burden
of both incidence and poor glycemic outcomes [ 4 , 5 ] . U.S. diabetes-related costs exceeded $400 billion in
2022 across all ages [ 6 ] , and pediatric-onset disease
contributes disproportionately to lifetime cost through its longer duration of
exposure.

Pediatric diabetes also differs biologically from adult-onset disease. Youth with
T2D show earlier micro- and macrovascular complications [ 7 , 8 ] and greater insulin resistance with hyperresponsive
beta cells relative to adults [ 9 ] , and the TODAY trial found durable glycemic
control from metformin alone in only about half of adolescents with
T2D [ 22 ] . T1D poses distinct challenges as well, including
glycemic variability, recurrent hypoglycemia, and early cardiovascular risk
emergence [ 11 , 12 ] . This heterogeneity motivates
precision approaches that stratify risk and guide individualized decisions.

blocks.en:
Pediatric diabetes care is delivered by a multidisciplinary team. The pediatric
endocrinologist interprets a child’s metabolic course alongside treatment history
and social circumstances, and integrates input from diabetes educators,
dietitians and social workers, each of whom contributes a different kind of
information.

blocks.en:
Machine learning (ML), by contrast, collapses this reasoning into a single
function approximation. Such models are widely applied to clinical
prediction from electronic health records (EHR) [ 13 , 14 ] , including in pediatric diabetes [ 15 , 16 ] , but treat prediction as pattern matching rather
than reasoning. They also leave largely untapped two modalities that plausibly
add value. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) captures temporal dynamics that static glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) cannot [ 17 , 18 ] , and social
determinants of health (SDOH) are documented in narrative notes but rarely
available as structured data [ 19 , 20 ] and are now extractable at
scale with LLMs [ 21 , 22 ] . Each has demonstrated
prognostic value on its own: CGM-derived features predict short-term
hypoglycemia and glycemic variability in type 1
diabetes [ 17 ] , and psychosocial burden is associated with worsening
glycemic control in youth with diabetes [ 5 ] . What is
unresolved is how much either adds beyond longitudinal structured EHR in
this setting, and in what representation. This gap between how clinicians
reason and how models predict motivates asking whether an LLM can reason
over the same multimodal evidence a clinician weighs.

Large language models (LLMs) with strong clinical knowledge [ 23 , 24 ] enable explicit, chain-of-thought reasoning over patient data [ 25 ] ,
and a natural next step is to decompose that reasoning across communicating
specialized agents [ 26 , 27 ] , by analogy to a care team.

blocks.en:
Recent systems apply this idea to clinical prediction, each covering a slice of
our problem. CARE-AD [ 28 ] predicts Alzheimer’s onset
from clinical notes, ColaCare [ 29 ] predicts in-hospital
mortality and readmission through multi-agent collaboration between LLMs and
trained EHR models, MDAgents [ 30 ] performs adaptive routing for
question answering and diagnosis, and MoMA [ 31 ] coordinates
modality-specialist agents that convert non-text modalities to text for
multimodal clinical prediction. These establish the
promise of agentic clinical prediction, yet enthusiasm has outpaced evidence.
The gains attributed to multi-agent debate are contested: majority voting, rather
than debate itself, accounts for most of them [ 32 ] , decision
protocols help unevenly across task types [ 33 ] , and
debate strategies do not reliably outperform simpler prompting at substantially
higher cost [ 3 ] . None of these systems has been evaluated in pediatric settings, where cohorts
are small and the outcomes of interest are uncommon, so a model has few training
examples to learn from. Pediatric diabetes is a demanding place to test them:
a child’s record is longitudinal but sparse, the complications being predicted
are uncommon, and the evidence a clinician would weigh is spread across
social-worker notes, structured EHR and, in T1D, continuous glucose
monitoring data. Four questions therefore remain open. First, can LLM reasoning
predict a child’s diabetes outcomes more accurately than a conventional
trained machine-learning model? Second, can the reasoning behind such a
prediction be trusted , that is, are the cited chart values real rather
than hallucinated? Third, do those cited values actually drive the prediction, or merely accompany it? Fourth, can a clinician follow the reasoning well enough to reach the same conclusion?

blocks.en:
We compare LLM reasoning with classical and temporal ML for pediatric diabetes outcome prediction. Using longitudinal Texas Children’s Hospital data, we predict seven type 2 and four type 1 diabetes outcomes at 24 months from the first 18 months of follow-up (Figure 1 ). We
introduce Cedar (Clinical Evidence-Driven Agent for Risk-prediction), a
single-model pipeline that reasons over structured EHR data, SDOH extracted from
social-worker notes and, for T1D, CGM, and cites the record values behind each
prediction so that a clinician can check them (Methods, Section 6).

预测,以便临床医生检查(方法,第6节)。

blocks.en:
We address these questions with four analyses. We compare Cedar with
classical and temporal ML across eleven cohort–outcome pairs in two cohorts, and
audit the faithfulness of the evidence it cites with established
rationale-evaluation protocols [ 8 , 7 ] .
Two pediatric endocrinologists review its reasoning blinded to the outcome, and an
information ablation measures how much of the predictive signal lies in the
outcome’s own history. We also test whether supplying a trained model’s score to Cedar as a tool improves prediction.

blocks.en: We built a benchmark in which the first three 6-month visit windows, covering months 0–18, predict each outcome at 24 months, across seven T2D and four T1D outcomes (Figure 1 ; Methods, Sections 1 to 3). Prevalence ranges from 58.7% for dyslipidemia to 8.9% for hypertension in T2D, and from 24.6% to 4.7% for the same two outcomes in T1D (Supplementary Table ). Cohort composition and feature availability are in Supplementary Tables and . Two companion studies describe these cohorts in more detail, in T2D (D. Palacios et al., manuscript in preparation) and in T1D (M. Ferm et al., manuscript in preparation).

distinguishes Cedar is that the rationale arrives as a fixed table of cited
features, visits and values (Methods, Section 6), so each claim resolves to a
record value a clinician can look up.

blocks.en: Two audits at different scales, both built on established rationale-evaluation protocols [ 8 , 7 ] , test whether that trace holds up.

blocks.en:
We first checked every scored patient-outcome record for fabricated evidence, 1,600 in T2D and 890 in T1D, comparing each cited feature, visit and value against the chart. Of 47,803 cited values in T2D
only 4 fail to match the record, three on metformin response and one on
microalbuminuria, and in T1D all 22,443 match. Fabricated evidence is therefore
essentially absent. This is a check on transcription rather than on clinical
judgment.

blocks.en:
We then asked whether the cited values drive the prediction or merely decorate
it, on a deeper counterfactual audit of up to 10 patients per outcome, giving 70
records and 2,050 cited features in T2D and 40 records and 1,046 cited
features in T1D. The cited evidence alone reproduces the prediction, with mean
sufficiency 0.95 in both cohorts, while no single citation is decisive, with mean
comprehensiveness 0.08 in T2D and 0.05 in T1D
(Figure 3 b). Masking the top cited values cumulatively
moves the prediction steadily further, from a mean change of 0.11 at the top
citation to 0.32 at the top ten, about five times the shift from masking the
same number of randomly chosen available values, 0.065 at the top ten
(Figure 3 c). Cited features therefore carry more of the
prediction than an equally sized arbitrary set, and the prediction rests on the
combined weight of many mutually supporting clues rather than on any one of
them, much as a clinician reasons.

blocks.en: Discussion
blocks.zh: 讨论情况

blocks.en:
We set out to test whether an evidence-citing LLM pipeline predicts pediatric diabetes outcomes better than trained machine learning, and whether its reasoning can be trusted. Across eleven cohort–outcome pairs in
two pediatric diabetes cohorts, Cedar beat trained classical and temporal ML,
with pooled T2D ROC-AUC 0.82 against 0.66–0.70. The accuracy benefit is
outcome-dependent, largest on sparsely screened endpoints such as dyslipidemia and
microalbuminuria and near zero on the best-powered outcomes, where a classical
model stays competitive at a fraction of the cost. Beyond accuracy, what Cedar adds is reasoning a clinician can use: two pediatric endocrinologists reading only its rationale reached the same
prediction in about nine cases in ten, and only 4 of
70,246 cited values did not match the record. Supplying the ML score as a tool added accuracy where the statistical model was strong, + 0.03 +0.03 ROC-AUC on that outcome.

blocks.en:
The pattern of gains across outcomes suggests an explanation. They are largest on dyslipidemia and microalbuminuria, outcomes that are screened sparsely, so few patients carry the measurement a trained model would learn from, whereas Cedar brings clinical priors through its guideline knowledge and its base model. On rare outcomes the trained models default to the majority class and rank near chance, and the two families make mistakes on different patients, which is why an ML score supplied as a tool helps only where that model is already strong. The information ablation supports this account. Most of the signal lies in the
outcome’s own recent history, consistent with trained models doing well where that
history is dense and poorly where it is sparse, and the clinical context matters
most when the history is thin. Reasoning over the whole record can therefore hold
accuracy for patients whose recent measurements are missing, a group that grows as
follow-up lengthens (Figure 1 b).

Several limitations bound these conclusions. The study is single-center and
retrospective, and the Cedar evaluation, though bootstrapped, uses adaptive
per-outcome test samples rather than the full cohort. Tool use raised accuracy on only one outcome, so its benefit is outcome-specific. Cost
estimates are based on vendor list prices, so the tiers should be read as orders of
magnitude. The temporal and external checks summarized in the Results do not replace
multi-site pediatric validation. Additional limitations and future directions are
detailed in Supplementary Note 1.

Two candidates are the raw social-worker notes in place of binarized SDOH factors, and a continuous-glucose foundation model [ 18 ] applied to the raw sensor trace.

trained statistical models we tested while producing reasoning that two pediatric
endocrinologists could follow and largely agreed with, and reasoning over the

practical foundation for pediatric prediction, and the direction worth building on
is richer evidence for the model to reason over.

blocks.en: Methods
blocks.zh: 方法

blocks.en:
All models are compared on a shared, held-out test set. For each
outcome, a single deterministic, prevalence-stratified train/test split
defines the test patients (random seed 42), and
every model family is scored on those identical patients with the same feature representation,
collinearity exclusions, and metrics. Trainable models are fit on the
training partition; the LLM configurations are inference-only. This matched
comparison is the basis for every head-to-head claim in this paper.

blocks.en: 2. Data structure and modalities

blocks.en:
Each patient has a matrix of features across 10 visit windows of 182 days (6-month intervals, 0–5 years post-diagnosis), organized into modality groups (Supplementary Table ). These are labs and vitals (18), medications (3, namely insulin, biguanide and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, GLP-1RA) and conditions (4, namely diabetic ketoacidosis, DKA, ketosis, retinopathy and neuropathy). The remaining groups are demographics (9, namely age at diagnosis, sex, Hispanic ethnicity, four race indicators, primary language and diabetes duration), SDOH (13 factors, enumerated below) and, for T1D only, CGM (20 per-visit glycemic metrics). The analysis-ready representation contains 47 features for T2D and
67 for T1D (cohort composition and feature availability in Supplementary
Tables and ).

blocks.en: CGM data are available only for T1D, which makes the two cohorts a natural modality contrast. Vendor exports differ in format and sampling, and none provides visit-aligned summaries, so we wrote our own extraction routine. It reads the raw sensor traces and reduces each patient’s readings to 20 metrics per 182-day visit window, covering glucose statistics, time in, above and below range, hypoglycemia episode counts and monitoring coverage (Supplementary Table ). The metrics and the glucose thresholds that define the time-in-range bands follow international consensus recommendations [ 40 ] rather than choices made for this study, so they are the features a clinician reading a CGM report would recognize. Because sensor wear is intermittent, the metric set also carries reading counts, monitoring duration and the fraction of the window missing, so every model can see how much data each metric rests on.

blocks.en: 3. Prediction targets, outcome definitions, and horizon
blocks.zh: 3个 预测目标、结果定义和前景

blocks.en:
We predict seven binary outcomes. Three are complications: hypertension (ICD diagnosis, or three consecutive outpatient blood-pressure readings above AAP-2017 age and sex thresholds) and dyslipidemia (non-HDL cholesterol ≥ \geq 145 mg/dL, an ICD E78.x diagnosis, or lipid-lowering therapy). The third is microalbuminuria (ICD diagnosis or urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) ≥ \geq 30 mg/g confirmed on two or more measurements, capped at 300). Four are treatment goals: optimal glycemic control (HbA1c < < 7%), insulin independence (off insulin, HbA1c < < 7%, no DKA), metformin response (on metformin alone with HbA1c < < 7%) and GLP-1RA response (on a GLP-1RA with HbA1c < < 7%). Each label is
1, 0, or not-assessable (null), the last excluded from that outcome’s
analysis. Because laboratory screening is not completed for every patient, the
assessable patients may differ from those who were not screened, which may limit
how far the results generalize.

blocks.en: 4. Reference baselines: classical ML and temporal ML
blocks.zh: 4个 参考基线:传统ML和时间ML

blocks.en:
Classical ML comprises three classifiers on the flattened feature matrix (all features by input visits). These are logistic regression (elastic net, L1 ratio 0.5, inverse regularization strength 1.0, SAGA solver), random forest (200 trees, max depth 10, min-leaf 5) and XGBoost (200 estimators, max depth 5, learning rate 0.1, subsample and column-sample 0.8). Temporal ML treats the visit history as a sequence. XGBoost-Temporal augments XGBoost with five engineered temporal features per base feature: last value, mean, standard deviation, first-to-last delta and ordinary least-squares slope. Four deep-sequence models complete the family. These are long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent unit (GRU) networks (2 layers, hidden size 64, dropout 0.3), a temporal convolutional neural network (CNN; 1-D convolution, 64 channels, adaptive pooling) and a Transformer (4-head attention, 2 layers, model dimension 64, learned positional embeddings). All four are trained for 100 epochs with Adam (learning rate 0.001, weight decay 0.0001) and class-weighted binary cross-entropy. Classical models use median imputation and standardization fit
on the training partition, and feature importances are collected on the
held-out folds.

blocks.en:
Cedar and every LLM configuration use Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Palantir Language Model Service identifier anthropic-claude-4-6-sonnet , version 1.151.0, accessed 2026-07-03), referred to below by its vendor short name claude-sonnet-4-6 . Models are called through the Palantir Language Model Service, within the
institution’s environment approved for protected health information, at temperature 0, except the self-consistency samples described below. The Results report the full Cedar pipeline (Section 6). For the reference benchmark in Supplementary Note 4 we also scored naive single-call configurations on the same patients. A direct configuration (“Vanilla”) gives one model the full multimodal record and asks for a probability, a binary prediction and a brief rationale. A chain-of-thought configuration (CoT) uses the same input with a structured step-by-step scaffold (metabolic, treatment, social, CGM for T1D, then severity), and Vanilla variants withhold the demographics and SDOH blocks or, in T1D, the CGM block.
A naive multi-agent configuration, in which modality-specialist agents’ free-text
findings are fused by an LLM synthesizer, underperformed and is reported only in
Supplementary Figure . To test whether results depend on
the base model, Cedar and the Vanilla configuration were re-run on all 11
cohort–outcome pairs with three further models spanning vendors and sizes, claude-haiku-4-5 , gemini-3-1-pro and the open-weight llama-3-3-70b , holding prompts, inputs and test sets fixed.

blocks.en: 6. Cedar : evidence-grounded, self-consistent clinical reasoning

blocks.en:
Cedar is a four-stage pipeline run per patient
(Figure 1 c). It runs on a single underlying model, and each stage targets one failure mode of naive prompting: missing domain priors, ungrounded reasoning, hallucinated evidence or miscalibration.

over a mean follow-up of 3.9 years [ 22 ] , so the injected
wording rounds the rate and shortens the horizon.

finally the free-text reasoning. S2, verification. Every citation is checked against the record by the

removed. In parallel a clinical evidence auditor pass reviews the same citations
and may issue a single revised probability. Both signals are reported separately in Supplementary Note 1. S3, self-consistency calibration. The
S1 prompt is resampled K = 3 K=3 times at temperature 0.7, and the mean of the

blocks.en:
Cost here is a token- and compute-based estimate, not a vendor bill, and it is
reported to separate the tiers by order of magnitude rather than to predict any
site’s budget. For LLM configurations, input and output tokens are tracked per call, priced at $3 and $15 per million tokens, the list price of the Claude Sonnet tier used here, and divided by the number of patients scored. Latency and call counts are logged separately. At these prices Cedar ’s five calls per patient (Section 6), with their long prompts and rationales, cost $0.099 per patient. That figure is indicative only, since actual spend depends on the provider, contract, model tier and any caching or batching, none of which are properties of the method. This gives $ 1.8 × 10 − 7 1.8\times 10^{-7} per patient for classical ML and $ 4.2 × 10 − 6 4.2\times 10^{-6} for temporal ML, which overstates their true marginal cost and so understates rather than inflates the Cedar -versus-ML gap.

blocks.en:
The primary metric is ROC-AUC, which is threshold-free and comparable across outcomes of very different prevalence, and Brier score is reported as an additional summary. ROC-AUC summarizes ranking across all thresholds, so it can stay high when decisions at a usable threshold are poor on a rare outcome. The benchmark was therefore repeated under Matthews correlation, balanced accuracy and positive-class F 1 F_{1} , each at a threshold selected on the training folds, which give the same ordering (Supplementary Note 1). Uncertainty is quantified by 2,000-iteration
patient-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. The shared held-out test
set is sized adaptively to the eligible population (50–250 patients, the
same test patients used for every model family) to keep per-outcome estimates
stable under imbalance, and tasks with fewer than 40 assessable patients or a
single class are skipped. The evaluation covers all seven outcomes for T2D
and the four outcomes that are clinically applicable in T1D (glycemic control,
hypertension, microalbuminuria, dyslipidemia); insulin independence, metformin
response and GLP-1RA response are T2D-specific. Classical and temporal ML baselines are run on the same eleven cohort–outcome pairs.

blocks.en: 11. Information-ablation experiment

blocks.en:
This experiment asks how much of each prediction rests on the outcome’s own
history. Each record is split into two channels. The outcome history holds the
laboratory values and diagnosis codes that define the outcome, at visits 1 to 3.
For the three treatment goals defined by glycemic control this is HbA1c, and for
insulin independence HbA1c with DKA codes. For the complications it is blood
pressure with the hypertension code, UACR, urine microalbumin and urine creatinine
with the microalbuminuria code, and the lipid panel with the dyslipidemia code. The clinical context holds every other
feature, namely demographics, SDOH, other laboratory values, other diagnosis codes
and medications. Medications that define an outcome are withheld from both
channels. Unlike the benchmark, which removes the defining laboratory value to
prevent collinearity (Section 3), the history reader sees it on purpose, since its
contribution is what the experiment measures. The label is always taken at
visit 4, after every visit shown.

Three readers run on claude-sonnet-4-6 at temperature 0 (Section 5). The
history reader sees only the outcome history and the context reader only the
clinical context. The combined reader sees both, together with the other two

of it is available. Each returns a probability from 0 to 100 with cited evidence,
and every citation is checked against the supplied features. The context reader is
called once per patient and its output is reused in every condition, so only the
history changes between conditions.

Two designs were run. The first scores the 1,600 T2D test patient-outcomes of the
benchmark with every available history value. The second withholds the history in seven conditions. Two show all three visits
of one source, laboratory values without codes or codes without laboratory values.
The other five restrict the history to visit 1, 2 or 3 alone, visits 1 and 2, or

condition does not apply to the three HbA1c-defined outcomes, which have no defining

in every condition. Discrimination is ROC-AUC per outcome, never pooled across
outcomes, with 1,000-resample paired bootstrap 95% confidence intervals that use
the same resampled patients for every reader.

Our error analysis shows a single LLM and Cedar misclassify almost the same

blocks.en:
One clarification about the faithfulness audit. Counterfactual intervention
measures faithfulness, how accurately a rationale reflects the computation that produced the prediction, whereas clinician rating measures plausibility and
clinical usefulness. The two can come apart [ 7 , §2] ,
so the two-specialist review reported in the Results
(Supplementary Figure 3 ) measures a different construct, not
a stronger version of the audit. The review bears this out: the two
endocrinologists agreed with Cedar ’s prediction on about nine cases in ten, yet on 29 of its 31
errors at least one of them reached the same incorrect call. A rationale can be
legible and well rated while the prediction it supports is wrong, which is why
the grounding and counterfactual audits, not the ratings, carry the
faithfulness claim. Because the two specialists largely reproduced Cedar ’s
errors, a rationale a clinician endorses is not yet a safeguard against a wrong
prediction. A larger review, and abstention when the record lacks the measurement
that defines the outcome, would test whether that gap can be closed.

blocks.en:
The main text reports these two experiments only by their result, so
their methods are given here. Verifier-gated refinement and diverse-reasoner ensembling
(“ Cedar v2”). A pre-specified screen asked whether two further internal mechanisms improve on the pipeline of Methods, Section 6, with the null
hypothesis that neither beats a single call by a meaningful margin. Five systems
were scored on the same fixed set of 60 held-out patients per outcome: a
Vanilla single call, Cedar as described, and three variants. Verifier-gated self-refinement re-runs the extractive-grounding check on S1’s citation table. If any cited triple is unverified, the offending citations are returned to the model by name, with an instruction to remove or correct them, re-examine the record and revise the probability, for at most two rounds, after which S2 and S3 proceed unchanged. In practice this gate almost never opened: first-pass
extractive grounding is already at ceiling, so no refinement round was triggered
in the screen (Supplementary Note 1). The diverse-reasoner ensemble replaces S1’s single
system prompt with three structurally distinct ones over an identical patient
prompt, directing the model to reason primarily from the longitudinal laboratory
and vital-sign trajectory, primarily from demographics, comorbid conditions and
social determinants, or primarily by applying the injected guideline knowledge. A meta-reasoner then receives all three reasoning chains with their probabilities and returns one integrated probability, instructed to weigh agreement and disagreement rather than to average. The unweighted mean of the three member
probabilities is retained as a secondary reference. The third variant combines
both mechanisms. The screen ran on the three highest-headroom T2D outcomes
(GLP-1RA response, hypertension, dyslipidemia), with both anchors re-scored on
the same 60 patients; promotion required a paired ROC-AUC difference whose
2,000-iteration bootstrap 95% interval excluded zero against both anchors. Neither addition met that rule (Supplementary
Figure 4 a).

blocks.en:
Four choices in those experiments need their reasoning stated. First, the
verifier-gated refinement arm returned a null that should be read as
uninformative rather than negative. First-pass extractive grounding is already at ceiling, so no refinement round was ever triggered in the screen, and the null says nothing about refinement in lower-grounding settings. Second, routing adds tokens, and across outcomes the
routed fraction spanned 0 to 1 at a cost of $0.091 to $0.104 per patient, so
the routing decision is not cost-free even where it is accuracy-neutral. Third,
the routed late-fusion combiner chose Cedar on all seven T2D outcomes, making
its T2D scores numerically identical to Cedar ’s, whereas in T1D it chose
classical ML on hypertension and on optimal glycemic control, which is why its
pooled T1D ROC-AUC (0.734) falls below Cedar ’s (0.759) in that cohort. Fourth,
the temporal split was cut so the partitions do not overlap in diabetes duration. In T2D the minimum training duration exceeded the maximum validation duration for all seven outcomes, with median duration 4.1–7.7 years in training against 2.4–3.4 years in validation. Training partitions held 140–801 patients
against 61–343 in validation.

reasoning harder over the same data, but serving as an auditable substrate that

single LLM to Cedar , is not about accuracy, since we detected no difference, but
about whether the case requires an auditable, record-grounded rationale. Cedar ’s five calls per patient buy that transparency, and on a weaker base

How many patients must be scored also matters, and the two regimes pull in
opposite directions. In a small, high-stakes setting, such as a rare-disease clinic or a new program with a few hundred patients, the total inference bill stays small

checkable rationale are easy to justify. At population scale that same rate
dominates costs, and a classical model that stays competitive on the well-powered
outcomes and needs no inference calls is the better default, with the LLM tier
reserved for the outcomes and patients where it earns its price. The cost
estimates therefore rank the tiers rather than decide between them.

The comparison
is deliberately asymmetric in one respect: Cedar ’s S0 stage injects
outcome-specific guideline priors (for example the TODAY finding on metformin
durability) that the statistical baselines never receive. This tests whether
guideline-grounded reasoning helps and is the kind of prior a clinician also
brings, so the gain should be read as “reasoning with clinical priors” rather
than “more of the same features.” The priors are general guideline statements,
never patient- or test-set-specific. We confirmed that the collinearity and
withheld-feature exclusions apply identically to the LLM prompts and the classical
feature matrices, that prompts use only input visits v1–v3 and never the target
visit, and that the shared train/test split is respected throughout. The trained
statistical models used fixed, standard hyperparameters (Methods, Section 4)
rather than an extensive search; nested hyperparameter optimization could
strengthen them, so the comparison is against well-configured rather than fully
optimized baselines.

blocks.en:
Two caveats remain. LLMs may have encountered guideline text or similar cohorts
during pretraining, which grounding and the withheld-feature design mitigate but
cannot eliminate. And on outcomes defined by a withheld lab or medication, the
model’s medical knowledge may let it reconstruct the target from correlated
laboratory values even with the defining feature removed, so we cannot fully
separate genuine reasoning from recalled priors about how such features co-occur. This caveat matters most for the largest LLM gains, such as dyslipidemia ( + 0.21 +0.21 ). A
third caveat is reproducibility: all results depend on specific hosted model
versions (Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the main pipeline; GPT 5.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.5
for SDOH extraction), and because these are updated over time, exact numbers may
not reproduce on later versions even with identical prompts. We report service
identifiers, versions and access dates to make the pipeline as reproducible as a
hosted service allows. Finally, Cedar here is a multi-stage pipeline over a
single model; whether heterogeneous agents would add value in larger-data regimes
remains open.

report. A further direction is an LLM re-ranking stage. Rather than combining families by voting or late fusion, a re-ranker could re-order candidate predictions from the cheaper tiers by reasoning jointly over the candidates and their grounding, a pattern that has improved list quality in
recommender and retrieval systems [ 11 ] . Because the re-ranker sees

ensemble cannot.

blocks.en:
Why are dyslipidemia and microalbuminuria so much more amenable to a language
model? Both are lab-defined renal or metabolic endpoints with sparse, irregularly
sampled screening labs, since urine microalbumin and lipid panels are typically
ordered at later surveillance visits rather than at diagnosis. We hypothesize the
gain reflects the LLM’s tolerance of missing and unevenly timed inputs, together
with clinical priors about which surrounding features (renal function, adiposity,
glycemic burden) covary with these endpoints, signal a fixed-schema classifier
trained on the same sparse columns cannot exploit. Masking those plausible
covariates, or inspecting the reasoning chains on correctly predicted cases, would
test this. The advantage does not track prevalence: it is largest on dyslipidemia
(58.7% prevalent) and microalbuminuria (25.6%) and near zero on optimal glycemic
control and insulin independence, the two best-powered outcomes. At a fixed 0.5
threshold the picture differs again, because on rare outcomes classical ML has the
lower error rate only by defaulting to the majority class (Supplementary
Figure 6 a). Finally, predicting at additional visits and
longer horizons, such as 5-year events, would establish whether the LLM advantage
persists as more temporal data accrue and the statistical baselines gain power.

Read together with the temporal check, the reasonable conclusion is that Cedar ’s edge is specific to the pediatric diabetes setting, with its sparse, scheduled, guideline-dense outpatient data, rather than general to clinical

the same boundary the modality ablation and the error analysis identify from inside
the pediatric cohorts. The comparison nonetheless remains asymmetric in one respect
worth stating: Cedar consumed no training labels on any of these tasks, while

Three limitations bound this benchmark. Task M-A has 34 test events, so the
sampling standard deviation of a 250-patient ROC-AUC is approximately 0.047 and
marginal gaps below roughly 0.09 are unresolvable there; only the paired
differences are interpretable. The multi-agent systems named in the Discussion were
not run, because they were not available in the credentialed analysis environment,
and a reimplementation that lost to Cedar would be evidence about the
reimplementation rather than about the published system. Finally, two failures are
worth recording because both were silent: an early run had a non-functioning
verification stage, which collapsed Cedar ’s fused probability onto its
first-pass estimate, and a Vanilla configuration whose outputs failed to parse on
every patient, yielding a ROC-AUC of exactly 0.500. Both were output truncation
rather than model behavior, and both were caught only by pre-specified mechanical
checks on a pilot subset before any metric was tabled. Had they been tabled,
they would have appeared as a large Cedar win.

List of suppfigures 2 Clinical economics: what paying for an LLM buys (T2D). These are
cost estimates rather than measured values (Methods, Section 8), which is
why the analysis appears here rather than in the main text. They are list prices
per token and per CPU-second at one point in time and exclude engineering, review
and infrastructure effort. Actual spend depends on the provider, the contract, the
model tier and any caching or batching applied, none of which are properties of
the method, so these panels separate the tiers by order of magnitude and should
not be read as a budget. The quantity that transfers between sites is the number
of model calls per patient: one for a single LLM, five for Cedar .
(a) Cost–performance Pareto frontier (log cost per patient against mean
ROC-AUC): classical ML anchors the cheap end, and both LLM tiers reach the top
accuracy band several orders of magnitude above it, with Cedar above a single LLM at the same accuracy, its extra calls buying auditability rather than discrimination. (b) Per-outcome cost-effectiveness of paying for a single LLM. The comparison is deliberately family-level, a single LLM against the best classical or temporal ML model, rather than a search for the single best model, because the
benchmark of Supplementary Note 4 finds that the inexpensive single LLM already
captures most of the LLM accuracy advantage (Supplementary
Figure 16 a). For each outcome the ratio is the ROC-AUC gain of
the single LLM ( ∼ \sim $0.006/patient) over the best ML model,
divided by the single-LLM cost per patient, i.e. ROC-AUC points gained per
dollar. Outcomes are sorted best to worst, each stem is annotated with the
underlying ROC-AUC gain, and color indicates whether that gain is statistically
distinguishable from ML (non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals, solid) or
numerical only (pale). We report the raw gain-per-dollar ratio rather than
applying a fixed “worth-it” AUC cut, which would be arbitrary. This panel
differs from Supplementary Figure 16 e, which compares best-ML and best-LLM AUC per outcome
without a cost axis.

List of suppfigures 6 Error stratification and selective prediction (supporting the
per-patient error analysis of Figure 4; the error-correlation
heatmap is in Figure 4a and not duplicated here).
(a) Error rate of each family within outcome-prevalence tertiles (T2D). At a
0.5 threshold, classical and temporal ML have a lower error rate on
low-prevalence outcomes only because they safely predict the majority class,
a near-chance ranking, whereas the LLMs attempt the rare positive calls. This
majority-class effect, not an ML discrimination advantage, is the mechanism
behind the cross-family error decorrelation. (b) Distribution of how many
of the four subgroups misclassify each patient: a large mass at 0 (all
correct) and a substantial “exactly 2 wrong” cluster, the two correlated
pairs failing as units.
(c, d) Selective prediction: risk–coverage curves (covered-set ROC-AUC
against the fraction of patients predicted, full coverage at left,
increasing abstention to the right), T2D and T1D. Four curves per cohort: a
single LLM’s bare probability (its distance from 0.5), Cedar ’s own bare
probability (“composite,” which folds in the two signals below but is
dominated by the bare-probability term since grounding is near-perfect), Cedar ’s self-consistency spread, and Cedar ’s verifier flag. Deferring
the least-confident patients raises covered-set AUC for the single LLM and for Cedar ’s bare probability, and the two track each other closely at every
coverage level. Self-consistency spread adds nothing beyond that shared
baseline in T2D and degrades it in T1D. The verifier flag is actively harmful as a confidence signal: in T2D, ranking on it alone lowers covered-set ROC-AUC by up to 0.14 at 40% coverage, consistent with a signal that almost never
fires and is therefore mostly noise. Useful abstention is a generic benefit of
any usable probability rather than something Cedar ’s verification or
self-consistency machinery adds. (e) The same comparison as a gain over full
coverage, T1D and T2D averaged. Neither signal Cedar produces internally, the
spread of its K = 3 K=3 self-consistency samples or the fraction of cited evidence its
verifier flags, improves on its own predicted probability read as a distance from
0.5 (gray dashed). Curves stop at 40% coverage, below which the retained subset
is too small to be reliable.

targeted tool-use result in Figure 4b). (a) The counterpart of Figure 4b on an outcome on which ML performs

score to Cedar as an in-context tool changes ROC-AUC significantly against

filled marker would mean the 95% confidence interval excludes zero). (b) The
behavioral signal: the mean shift the injected score induced in Cedar ’s output
relative to the no-tool run (x) versus the fraction of resulting overrides that were

bad one, though it can over-trust a noisy score. This is a hypothesis-generating result on a
single ML-competitive outcome, not a general accuracy claim; it motivates the future
direction of designing outcome- and modality-specific tools for the agent
(Discussion).
